rounds.message: How should I pray when God feels silent?

turn_selected.reason: Papnoute's formation - the Desert tradition of extended silence, prayer in absence, and the mystical encounter with God in emptiness - is the most directly positioned voice to address this question. Desert monasticism developed its deepest practices precisely around persevering in prayer when God feels hidden or withdrawn.

voice.speaker: desert
voice.text:
We named stillness - hesychia - as something sought on purpose, and we meant that plainly. Not the silence imposed on you from outside, but the quiet you make room for, even when it feels empty at first. One of us taught it this way: a monk's whole attention should be fixed on one point, the way a builder who wants to raise a round arch must constantly draw a line from its exact center - every thought returning there, to the recollection of God, no matter how far it wanders. That is not a feeling. It is a discipline, kept up whether the feeling comes or not.

The silence you are naming - God feeling absent - we would have called it one of the thoughts that trouble you, and we fought those the same way we fought fear or pride: by standing guard over them, catching them early, while they are still small. You do not argue with the thought. You return to the one point, again and again, the way the builder returns to the center. The deepest among us - and only a few of us went this deep - held that God is known less by argument than by a long stilling of the passions that crowd the mind, and that in the quiet earned that way, something of him becomes visible that was not visible before. We cannot promise you the feeling will come when you want it. We can tell you that the practice is kept whether it does or not.

voice.text:
Prayer, as we held it, was not mainly speaking to God. It was the soul turning to attend to what God is already saying. That is not a feeling either - it is a direction, held whether the feeling comes or not, and I hear something honest in what has just been said to you about the discipline kept up when nothing seems to move.

But we would add this. The silence you are naming may be the very place where formation is happening - not its absence. Our teacher Clement wrote that the Instructor cures the soul's passions 'by means of exhortations' - the Word himself is at work in what feels like emptiness. And one of our students, Gregory, said love for the Word came to him almost from the side, like a spark landing on his inmost soul while he studied under a teacher: he was not straining after God, he was being befriended. The transformation we spoke of was never something forced. It was something undergone, often slowly, and the silence may be part of the undergoing.

One more thing, because it touches what you are asking. We kept a tradition about the apostle John and a young man who had fallen away and become a robber. John rode out to the mountain, old as he was, and when the young man fled, John called after him: 'Why do you flee from me, child? There is still hope of life for you'. The point for you is this: the one you are trying to pray to does not wait for you to feel his presence before he comes looking. The silence is not his abandonment.

voice.text:
What has been said here touches what we held, though we come at it from a different place. The turning to attend, kept whether the feeling comes or not - yes, that is close to what we meant. And the Word at work in what feels empty - we would not have said it that way, but we did hold that the struggle itself is where the work happens, not only its resolution.

What we would add is this. The silence you feel may not be God's absence so much as your own passions filling the space where he might otherwise be heard. One of the deepest among us - and we should say plainly, he was unusually educated, not our common voice - taught that apatheia, freedom from what drives you, is what lets the soul see what was always there. That seeing was held to be known in real experience and feeling, not only believed. But the feeling comes at the far end of a long discipline, not at the start of it.

We cannot tell you God will feel present tomorrow if you pray rightly tonight. What we can tell you is that the quiet you make room for, kept up whether he feels near or not, is itself the practice - and that what crowds him out may be more your own than his.

voice.text:
What I heard spoken just now - that the silence may be your own passions filling the space where God might otherwise be heard - that is true, and we would say it differently but mean something close. We called it the soul's disordered wanting, turned toward lesser goods when it was made for God himself. The discipline named here, the long quiet that clears that space, we honored - though we came at it through argument and Scripture more than through the desert's silence.

But here is what I would most want you to carry from what was said. The struggle itself is where the work happens, not only its resolution - that line is worth keeping. We held the same thing, though we called it by another name: paideia, God's own patient training of the soul. The silence you feel, the emptiness, may be exactly the place where God is teaching you something your earlier prayers could not reach. Our teacher wrote that every threat and pain that comes from God is never to injure but always to heal. The desert voice has just told you plainly: the quiet is kept whether the feeling comes or not. We would add: it is kept because the Teacher is at work in it, whether you can see his hand yet or not.

You have been given two honest answers from two different ways of walking the same road - one through argument and Scripture, ours; one through the long quiet, theirs.
